title: Posted an analysis on The Big Walk situation, and it wasn't accepted by everyone
author: lonelyroom-eklaghor
selftext:
Here's the post:

Title: Analysis on the sitatuation around The Big Walk (the full post is long, please read it, 

(yes, this is the only place where I had mistakes)

Let's start the post.

\---

Oh boy, we have a lot of discuss. Analyses like these are important in order to understand the Internet properly now.

\[...\]

For years now, those who are up-to-date with the gamedev news know how there are review-bombings going all over. The review bombings are starting from some specific discord servers I don't want to name.

A lot of indie gamedevs have reported how even a slight disclosure of generative AI is leading people to give negative reviews from the ones who have only played a game for a few minutes.

Again, from Wikipedia:

\>House House did not have an internal AI policy in place while developing the game, which they would later describe as "a failure".

There are some more nuances to this.

Here's the full statement from "House House" (TL;DR below):

\>Was AI used to make Big Walk?

\>In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs. In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.

\>The primary use case for House House’s use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code. If you’re technically-minded, and curious, here’s an example. We needed to cull shadow casters by distance from the camera, but Unity URP only allows culling shadow casters by distance in camera forwards, so shadow casters behind the player were being rendered at an infinite distance. This made our game run 50% slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset. We researched the problem extensively, and we looked at the URP code ourselves, but we couldn’t find a way. Then, we were able to speak directly to an engineer at Unity, who asked around and ultimately concluded that what we wanted wasn’t possible. Finally, we posed the question to an LLM chatbot. After a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked. This fix represented about 10 lines of code inside URP.

\>We originally wrote a version of the above disclosure as it was a suggested part of our IGF submission. We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest.

\>This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as “inevitable”. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.

\>Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards.

The TL;DR is: in the whole day cycle, the gameplay was slower when the sun used to rise or set in-game. They exactly knew where the bug was. However, they couldn't resolve it at all. They talked to an Unity engineer, and the Unity Engineer concluded it's impossible to mitigate the exact bug they had. Finally, they went to an LLM and after probing some stuff, they had a fix. They had to modify the fix before adding it to the game. "The fix" we are talking about consisted of only 10 lines in the final product. Note that Steam doesn't require disclosure of code or chatbot usage.

To give an idea to the non-coding audience of what 10 lines of code in rendering pipeline means, it is really essential, because it can make or break a game. But if we are considering the number of lines of LLM code, even slightly beginner-level programs have 40-50 lines of code.

So, a very small LLM fix inside a huge game that didn't require a Steam disclosure. This outrage against LLMs made me angry becuase we have seen how devs like YandereDev or PirateSoftware code, or the mindset of Theo. [Yandere Dev has very questionable coding choices](https://youtu.be/dlrjDvS7wxo) (just like the toothbrush fiasco; I had a headache looking at \`MonoBehaviour.Update()\`), [PirateSoftware's switch statements have literally 1000 cases](https://youtu.be/6KtzADIW0tg) (that's not the way to write clean code), Theo literally said something along the lines of "if you understand code, your code is not professional/deployable enough".

*Let me tell you all that neither AI creates slop code everytime, nor slop code is created by AI everytime.* Read that again.

LLMs are "prone" to creating slop code. So are humans.

We can teach humans. We can train AI. Critical bugs in foundational software like Linux are being mitigated daily after Mythos. You guys have heard of the NVIDIA scandal; back in the days,[ there was Jia Tan. Google "xz-utils backdoor".](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XZ_Utils_backdoor) Every day, kernel devel people are getting CVEs greater than 9.0/10. Every day, Linux is patching a potential xz-utils. Almost every website is running Linux; every top 500 supercomputer is running Linux. No wonder the infra is critical.

I have a lot to talk about, but it feels really disheartening when some people in certain discord servers have a tendency of punching down small gamedevs, whilst AAA not being criticized using LLM code for the game you guys are waiting for.

Within a few years, the Internet has become so fucking low-trust that people are punching down the small ones. I understand that it might be due to the amount of income artists these days are getting, but this is not the way. I am one of the first people talking about soul in AI art, but AI code CANNOT BE JUDGED THAT WAY. That's also a form of conflation. I don't want to see gamedevs-mitigating-game-breaking-bugs-through-LLMs being controversial.

# Conclusion

On a serious note:

We the coders are caught in a crossfire. We cannot talk about what we have built anymore without being accused of "AI slop". Please understand that we are not an artist's enemy. I am a CS undergrad right now and I am not a gamedev, but I do maintain some software and websites in my freetime. I can write code without even needing a proper IDE. Yet this time, it's really difficult for me to show the thing I am building for my final year research project, because even making apps are considered low-effort now.

You guys see how coders are being laid off left and right. Bad reviews are not a meagre matter; they impact a person's morale and sales. I am properly learning how to code simply because I want to get financial assistance sometime for using my intellect by slogging on a 5-legged chair for 30-40 years, so that I can get an armchair for myself after that. Ik I took a wrong choice, but I took this undergrad degree as a challenge; wanted to see what I do in 4 years.

For programmers, LLMs actually makes menial tasks easier. Moreover, one should consider the conficts of interest associated with the research papers.

Lastly, I just want to say: House House didn't have to make an internal policy on AI for A BUG FIX. Maybe you guys really deserve YandereDev's toothbrush.

comments.author: unfamily_friendly
comments.body: The question is not how AI was used. Everyone in this chain could lie. The game might be 100% vibe coded, and no way to find out. The real question is, how much did it affect the sales? If affect at all. Like, did people stopped buying their game? Or asked Steam for refund out of 2 weeks window?
